children.translated_text: I bow to that mighty splendor of Garuḍa, which is the fitting ally of <s>Viṣṇu</s> for the welfare of the three worlds,

children.text: sāpatnamindrasya ca tat vande gārutmataṃ mahaḥ ||
children.translated_text: and which is also the rival of <s>Indra</s>.

children.text: kāmaśāstrānabhijñānāṃ kāmaḥ kiṃ nu na gocaraḥ
children.translated_text: Is desire not within the range even of those who do not know the science of desire?
Even so, the treatise was composed by sages for the knowledge of its true principles.
In just the same way, though the essence of game is familiar even to the lowliest person,
it reaches a special delight in the heart of one who knows falconry.
Therefore, for the production of genuine rasa, the useful science of falconry
is here distinguished from hunting, both in brief and in detail.
For men, for the attainment of enjoyments seen in former times, and for the delight of the mind, amusements

children.text: sṛṣṭā viśvasṛjā kārtsnyāt ke tān gaṇitumīśate ||
children.translated_text: were created in their entirety by the creator of the universe; who can count them?

children.text: teṣu ye'ṣṭādaśa proktā vyasanānīti yān viduḥ
children.translated_text: Among them, those eighteen which are declared and which people know as vices
without them there is neither the fruit of the senses nor the grounds of relish.

children.text: sevyamānāḥ sukhāyālaṃ bhavanti prāṇināṃ ca te
children.translated_text: When they are practiced, they are fully conducive to the happiness of living beings,
according to the proper time and according to due nourishment, especially for kings.
They are constantly condemned by the authors of treatises as “vices,”
and histories too are heard which show the ruin of those attached to them.
If women with indolent eyes smiling with passion were to be avoided entirely,

children.text: punnāmno narakāt trātrī bhavet kva janiraurasī ||
children.translated_text: where would there be a legitimate son, the rescuer from the hell called <s>Put</s>?
If hunting were absolutely forbidden, then where, as means for sacrifices and the like,
would meat, skins, horns, and so forth, enjoined by rule, be obtained?
Through the practice of sleep by day there is the destruction of ailments such as indigestion,
and likewise of the body here, the instrument for accomplishing the three aims of life.

children.text: tasmāt sarvātmanā tyājyaḥ saṅga eveti niścayaḥ
children.translated_text: Therefore what is to be abandoned in every way is attachment alone; this is the settled conclusion.
For the sayings of the <s>Bhāgavata</s> state just this: bondage arises through attachment.
The mere abandonment of actions is solely for liberation;
but the performance of the action prescribed for one’s birth-group is indeed desired for the three aims of life.
That renunciation would be accomplished by actions of mind, speech, and body;
from that, when performed, would arise the <s>brahman</s> beyond the reach of words.
If, for the highest good, a wish to abandon attachment to actions should arise
in a creature through a mass of merit, then he should undertake renunciation.
Enjoyment too is heard to be a cause for the exhaustion of actions, as when
the wise <s>Saubhari</s> pursued objects of sense in order to be freed from bondage.
And in the same way verses are heard, uttered by the ancestors,
which, for the true welfare of the dispassionate <s>Ruci</s>, entered his heart.
Former action is exhausted day and night through enjoyments,
through one’s own pleasures and pains, my child, being of the nature of merit and demerit for men.
When your entitlement has been exhausted, knower of dharma, then you will attain tranquility.

children.text: tathā bhāgavataṃ vākyaṃ śrūyate cārjunaṃ prati ||
children.translated_text: Likewise a statement of the <s>Bhāgavata</s> is heard, addressed to <s>Arjuna</s>:

children.text: kuru karmaiva tasmāttvaṃ karma jyāyo hyakarmaṇaḥ
children.translated_text: Therefore perform action alone; action is superior to inaction.

children.text: śarīrayātrāpi ca te na prasidhyed akarmaṇaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Even the maintenance of your body would not succeed through inaction.
In other treatises also many utterances of speakers of truth are heard,
urging action for those who observe the conduct of the householder’s stage.
A householder whose wealth has been acquired justly, who is devoted to knowledge of truth, who loves guests,
who performs śrāddha and speaks truth, is liberated even while being a householder.
By such Vedic statements and the like it is accepted that even the fruits born of action

children.text: bhogaḥ phalānāṃ prāptānāṃ sa tu saṃgavivarjitaḥ ||
children.translated_text: are to be enjoyed when they have been obtained, but that enjoyment is without attachment.
King <s>Janaka</s> is heard of as intent on protecting his subjects;
while enjoying enjoyments he was fit for liberation, and non-attachment was the cause there.
This too is a naturally beautiful path to final release;
and heaven is easy for men through the proper observance of what is prescribed for their own birth-group.
One intent on it should perform action that leads to heaven, fame, and long life;
“performing actions here alone” and so forth is also the fixed teaching in the Veda.

children.text: sukṛtaiḥ prāpyate sampat sā ca bhogāya ceṣyate
children.translated_text: By good deeds prosperity is obtained, and that is held to be for enjoyment;
and that enjoyment is attended by the eighteen kinds of vices.

children.text: pṛthak tebhyo bhīmarūpo na kutrāpi pratīyate
children.translated_text: Apart from them, no fearsome form is perceived anywhere;
even what consists of food, garlands, sandal, and the like is remembered as serving their purpose.
Therefore spring, the rainy season, sandal paste, moonrise, and the like
bring joy to those embraced by their beloveds, but distress to those separated from them.

children.text: dharmadrumasya phalamarthamudīrayanti śāstreṣu niścitadhiyo hi yathāgamena
children.translated_text: Those whose minds are certain in the treatises declare, according to scripture, that wealth is the fruit of the tree of dharma;

children.text: taṃ dānabhogavidhaye sujano niyuṅkte samyak tayoḥ pariṇatiḥ suṣamānupaiti ||
children.translated_text: the good man applies it to giving and enjoyment, and the proper maturation of both attains beauty.

children.text: iti śrīkūrmācalādhipatirudradevaviracite śyainike śāstre karmānuṣañjanaḥ prathamaḥ paricchedaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Thus, in the Śyainikaśāstra composed by the illustrious <s>Rudradeva</s>, lord of <s>Kūrmācala</s>, the first section, “The Connection with Action,” is complete.
Now the group of eighteen, beginning with harshness of speech and the rest,
is described both by name and according to whether each is to be rejected or not rejected.
Harshness in speech and in punishment, jealousy, fault-finding, rash violence,
spoliation of wealth, slander, and anger itself are born of anger.
Women, gambling, liquor, singing, dancing, instrumental music, useless wandering,
speaking ill behind one’s back, daytime sleep, and hunting: these are born of desire.
Speech that is obscene and harsh is held to be harshness of speech;

children.text: daṇḍeṣu vyavahāre ca śobhate nānyadā kvacit ||
children.translated_text: it is proper in punishments and legal proceedings, but nowhere else at all.
Punishment inflicted on one undeserving, and very severe punishment, is called harshness of punishment;
it is fully suited to producing majesty in a crisis, but should not be practiced at other times.
Jealousy is inability to endure the prosperity of others; it is commended with regard to an enemy,
because, when thus stimulated, one strives for his destruction.
The imputation of faults onto what is virtuous and the like is called fault-finding;
but it is commended among jesters and others in private conversation.
When it is being performed, its elaboration should be observed in dramas and the like.
And in narratives and the like also, according to the combination of concise and expanded treatment,
an action that creates doubt about life, when done, is called rashness.
In times of calamity that may serve for distinction, but at another time it becomes a cause for ridicule.
Scattering, failure to accept, instruction given to an unfit recipient,
or the spoiling of gift, acceptance, and purpose by cutting at the root:
that should, with effort and through trustworthy men, be caused to be done in an enemy's territory.
The disclosure of others' faults is called slander.
All that should be heard from the mouth of a spy, and then with one's own understanding,
after confirming it by other spies also, one should then undertake a countermeasure.
Cruelty in inflicting punishments and the like is called anger by the wise.
One should employ it toward those who are always harmful, but not toward others.
Endowed with good marks, skilled in the arts, capable, possessed of good fortune,
and endowed with age and modesty: such a woman is called a woman by the wise.
She is the means to the three aims of life and the splendor of the householder stage,
through childbirth, household equipment, sight, delight of the mind, and the like.
This was also formerly said by <s>Kumāra</s> when <s>Agastya</s> asked:
where there is mutual favor between husband and wife, there the three aims of life increase.

children.text: dharmmādartho'rthataḥ kāmaḥ kāmaḥ strībhyo na cānyataḥ
children.translated_text: From <s>dharma</s> comes wealth, from wealth comes desire, and desire comes from women and not otherwise.
Therefore, ah, the fruit of the tree of <s>dharma</s> is a loving woman with beautiful hips.
Therefore a man should in every way make her attached to him,
abandoning unrestrained conduct in matters such as the experience of love.
And the love that belongs mutually to husband and wife whose minds are fixed on no other,
known only to themselves and not to be described, that touch is said to be desire.
In the oceans of pearl-like sayings of the virtuous, of <s>Vyāsa</s>, and of <s>Vālmīki</s>,
its extensive elaboration is by union and separation in love.
Play, whether with living or lifeless things, preceded by a stake, is called gambling with dice.
When well employed, it comes about for the increase of wealth and the growth of pleasure.
The substance by drinking which one becomes intoxicated is called liquor.
Even that is commended by those who know in illnesses that are incurable.
That which is to be sung by one with a pleasing throat, joined with rhythm and pitch,
and suitable for graceful dance: those who know song understand that to be music.
And, according to occasion, that is a means to the four aims of life.
In singing, the accomplishment of wealth and pleasure is seen directly.
The accomplishment of <s>dharma</s> and liberation is as stated by <s>Bharata</s>,
and likewise by the sage <s>Yājñavalkya</s> and by others such as <s>Nārada</s>.

children.text: gītajño yadi gītena nāpnoti paramaṃ padam
children.translated_text: If one who knows song does not attain the supreme state by song,
then, having become an attendant of <s>Rudra</s>, he rejoices together with him through that very song.
What is vigorous <s>tāṇḍava</s> and what is graceful dance consisting of expressive gesture,
joined with proper movements and rhythm, is called dance of two kinds.
Instrumental music is said to be fourfold, divided into stretched-string and other classes.
The purpose of dance and instrumental music should be understood to be the same as that of song.
Approaching gardens, cities, and the like without any business
is idle wandering; but it is praised for the removal of bodily sluggishness.
Indirect blame, whose meaning is clear, is intended to deceive.

children.text: sarvartuṣu divāsvapnaḥ so'pi vyaktārtha eva hi
children.translated_text: Day-sleep in all seasons: that too has an evident meaning indeed.
And it is good for children, for those afflicted with diarrhea, for the emaciated, and for those with indigestion.

children.text: ta ete saptadaśa ca mṛgayāṣṭādaśī tathā
children.translated_text: These are the seventeen, and hunting is the eighteenth;

children.text: heyāheyāḥ purā prāha bhīṣmo dharmātmajaṃ yathā ||
children.translated_text: long ago <s>Bhīṣma</s> declared them to <s>Dharmātmaja</s> as things to be rejected and not to be rejected.
And all vices you should abandon, O giver of abundant gifts,

children.text: na caiva na prayuñjīta saṃgaṃ tu parivarjayet ||
children.translated_text: yet one should not entirely fail to use them; one should avoid attachment.

children.text: itthamatra paricintya lāghavaṃ gauravaṃ ca guṇayogataḥ pṛthak
children.translated_text: Thus, having considered here lightness and gravity separately according to the presence of qualities,
one should set them to use as appropriate for pleasing the world, while removing mere attachment.

children.text: iti śrīrudradevaviracite śyainike śāstre vyasanaheyāheyatānirūpaṇo dvitīyaḥ paricchedaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Thus ends the second section, the determination of vices as to what is to be rejected and not rejected, in the <s>Śyainikaśāstra</s> composed by the illustrious <s>Rudradeva</s>.
Now, then, hunting too, in concise and expanded treatment,
though one, is explained here as eightfold and manifold.
For the accomplishment of meat and other purposes, and for pleasure through various means,
the killing of any living creature is called hunting.
Where there is killing of living creatures, there is a succession of faults.
Animals fit for sacrifice, domestic and wild, are said to be fourteen.
The killing of these when they have not been consecrated by sprinkling becomes a fault.

children.text: asmin arthe purā ślokā yathā dvaipāyanoditāḥ ||
children.translated_text: On this matter there are ancient verses as spoken by <s>Dvaipāyana</s>:
in the dialogue between <s>Pāṇḍu</s> and <s>Kindama</s>, in connection with the killing of deer,

children.text: śatrūṇāṃ yā vadhe vṛttiḥ sā mṛgāṇāṃ vadhe smṛtā ||
children.translated_text: the practice that applies to the killing of enemies is remembered as applying to the killing of deer.

children.text: rājñāṃ mṛga na māṃ mohāt tvaṃ garhayitumarhasi
children.translated_text: O deer, you should not reproach kings out of delusion;

children.text: achadmanā māyayā vā mṛgāṇāṃ vadha iṣyate ||
children.translated_text: the killing of deer is accepted, whether without concealment or by stratagem.
The seer <s>Agastya</s>, while sitting in a sacrificial session, practiced hunting,
sprinkling wild animals belonging to all the gods in the great forest.
Because of <s>Agastya</s>'s sprinkling, violence does not apply in hunting.
For domestic animals, sprinkling is praised in sacrifices and the like according to rule.
For wild animals, killing is praised because of <s>Agastya</s>'s sprinkling.
And histories are heard concerning kings in the practice of it.
Where, from exercise and from exertion, there is on the contrary the experience of fatigue,

children.text: yatra tatra sukhāyeti vyarthaṃ cet tatra kathyate ||
children.translated_text: if it is said there that it is for pleasure, that is pointless.
Just as forced kissing, embracing, and the like of a proud woman,
though achieved through effort, does not truly produce inner delight,
just as a blow from nails, teeth, and the like in the battle of love
So too here there is no injury or pain, because of the absorption in rasa.

children.text: iti siddhaṃ lakṣaṇaṃ hi mṛgayāyāḥ puroditam
children.translated_text: Thus the established definition of hunting has been stated above.
Now the distinction among its eight kinds is set forth.
Like <s>Hara</s>'s form, a single beloved woman, according to differences of condition,
is enough for eightfold rasa; just so hunting too is considered eightfold.
One is mounted hunting, another is netted hunting, another is the kālyā hunt, another is the yāvaśī hunt;
another is dependent hunting, another is track-watching, and another is hunting with packs of dogs.
The eighth is the falcon's strike: these have been named in order.
Now their own defining marks, and how they are to be carried out, are stated.
In that hunt in which deer, fleeing while horses serve as the means,

children.text: vadhyante hi mṛgā yasyāṃ sāśvīnā rasaśevadhiḥ ||
children.translated_text: are killed with arrows and the like, that mounted hunt is a treasury of rasa.
Ground without trees, mud, or stones, and without gaps, is commended;
and the proper time is held to be from the end of the middle of winter up to the middle of <s>Jyaiṣṭha</s>.
Through good practice of it there arise reduction of fat and lightness in the body,
increase of strength, compactness, firmness, and skill of the inner fire;
endurance of hunger, thirst, cold, heat, laziness, wakefulness, and the like;
skill with moving targets and so on, and an increase of energy;
the manifestation of one's own courage, and knowledge of the mental movements of living beings;
such and similar excellences of qualities arise for the perfection of the self.
Likewise there is also the acquisition of <s>dharma</s> by killing wolves, tigers, and the like,
and by protecting crops and so forth through the killing of deer and other animals;
by inspecting forests useful for many purposes,
by frightening thieves, and also by pleasing the forest people.
So too wealth is acquired by pursuing the frontal globes of rutting elephants,
and by obtaining horns, hides, musk, pearls, feathers, and the like.
Through eating good meat from boars, quails, and other animals,
and through the abundance of heightened vigor, there is also a plentiful intensification of desire.
Rasa, pride, and self-assertion are said to be the whole substance of love.
Therefore, for one wearied by hunting deer, an anointing with sandal and the like,
the massaging of the limbs by the hand-sprouts of doe-eyed women,
drinks such as pañcasāra, and repeated breezes from palm-leaf fans are prescribed.
For by pride of mind one attains connection in the way appropriate to the relation;

children.text: anyadā na tathā yena tena kāmaikavedanam ||
children.translated_text: not otherwise, and for that reason love has a single felt experience.
Some designation as 'woman-hunting' is seen in the nourishing of rasa;
indeed the authors of śāstra have shown just this much subtle distinction.
In union, habitual delight is unsurpassed in lovemaking;
and because of the predominance of rasa, the determinants and consequents are the same in the two.
They are observed, as appropriate, through union and separation.
Their full treatment with regard to women is large in works on dramaturgy and poetics,
and is seen in the <s>Kāmaśāstra</s> and other texts; therefore it is not stated here.
But for hunting it is stated briefly, for the sake of understanding.
The seizure, by hawks and other birds, of birds and the like released from a distance,
and the archer's forceful success of the arrow on a moving or unmoving target,
express the highest delight through tears, horripilation, and a choked voice;
and the loss of that very thing is described as separation.
For it produces conjecture, recollection, pallor, lamentation, and the like.
Thus, from this and similar reasoning, there is a resemblance between hunting and a woman.
Therefore this too is praised as a means for the three aims of life.
When the force has assembled with sufficient space and has been extended facing the wind,
it succeeds without difficulty by an advance toward the deer.
For an advance upon a rhinoceros, only five or six mounted men are recommended.
Tractable horses are commended, those trained in going forward and coming back.

children.text: tvarayā pṛṣṭhato vedhyaḥ kṣudraśaktyā tu sādinā ||
children.translated_text: The animal should be pierced quickly from behind by a rider of limited strength.
If it turns back, then the rider who goes in front of it
must promptly act with confidence in his own horse.
When it advances toward him, it should be pierced from behind by another;
or else it should be pierced from the side with arrows by the best bowmen.
Even a proud lord of beasts is killed by bowmen on swift horses,
by a target that is both apparent and unapparent, as if it were a cat.

children.text: sā sajālā kūṭavṛttyā yasyāṃ nighnanti vai mṛgān
children.translated_text: That hunt is the netted one, in which they kill deer by deceptive practice,
and also make captures of fish, shells, otters, and pearl-oysters.
In it an endless variety of implements used by men is observed;
its practice is seen among lowly people, chiefly niṣādas.
It is especially useful for accomplishing such things as elephant-capture with ease.

children.text: kāraṇīyā nṛpaiḥ sā tu mahodayakarī yataḥ ||
children.translated_text: But kings should have it performed, since it produces great prosperity.
Even conduct by concealment in this case is not held to be a fault.
On this point there is <s>Vālmīki</s>'s example in the killing of <s>Vālin</s>.
With nets, traps, nooses, and various devices,
many men, hidden and unseen, capture wondrously;
and those skilled in the law of hunting also pierce the animals from the front.
Deer catch deer, and birds catch birds;
through the application of training, that too falls within netted hunting.
The kālyā hunt is accomplished by being driven together by many men, with others at the rear and others stationed in front.

children.text: sādhyate yā pṛthaklīnaiścaturdhā sā tu bhidyate ||
children.translated_text: It is divided into four kinds, with separate concealed positions.
When antelopes, being driven with loud calls against the wind by two or three men,
are killed by releases made in three dispersed directions, that is the many-eared kind.

children.text: pṛṣṭhato nibiḍībhūtaiḥ kālyante yatra vai mṛgāḥ
children.translated_text: Where deer are driven from behind by men massed densely together,
and where they are caught by men concealed at the foot of trees, that is the root-attached kind.
When, from far away, animals of many species are gradually drawn into a circle, contracted together,
and confined in one place,
and there they are killed in many ways by many men with swords and the like,

children.text: mahākālyeti sā proktā sidhyate sā nṛpādibhiḥ ||
children.translated_text: that is called <s>mahākālī</s>; it is accomplished by kings and others.
Another, called <s>gajakālī</s>, is carried out with elephants, horses, and the like,
in the summer season, by blocking the sparse water supplies.
Men skilled in carrying out the fourfold <s>kālī</s>

children.text: yujyante kālane mokṣe śarāṇāṃ cānyathā nṛṇām
children.translated_text: are fit for the timing and release of arrows; otherwise, for men,
the effort would be fruitless, and destruction is seen among one's own people themselves.
Where animals to be killed are indicated merely by the movement of barley, grain, and the like that has been put out,

children.text: vadhyante yatra vai vadhyā yāvaśī sā prakīrtitā ||
children.translated_text: and there the proper quarry is killed, that is called <s>yāvaśī</s>.
It is accomplished by just two or three horsemen skilled in releasing arrows,
through the movement of the falcon and by observing the shaking of the grain.
Although it causes great exertion, it arises for delight.
Where a single bowman, having concealed himself and depending on the expectation of deer and the like,

children.text: dhanvī vidhyati digdhena sā sāpekṣā smṛtā budhaiḥ ||
children.translated_text: shoots with a poisoned arrow, that is remembered by the wise as <s>sāpekṣā</s>.

children.text: vibhītakādau kṣetre vā nipāne sā tu sidhyati
children.translated_text: It succeeds near vibhītaka trees, in fields, or at watering places,
and gives easy success for killing lions and the like among cows, carcasses, and similar baits.
Where deer are killed by following their tracks,

children.text: padaprekṣā ca sā proktā dvidhā sāpi prayujyate ||
children.translated_text: that is called <s>padaprekṣā</s>; it too is practiced in two ways.
When, after searching all around for a long time with dogs and making harsh effort,

children.text: vadhyate hi mṛgo yasyāṃ śvapadaprekṣikā hi sā ||
children.translated_text: a deer is killed, that is indeed <s>śvapadaprekṣikā</s>, tracking by dogs.
Where a bowman, with effort and skill, searches by himself

children.text: suptaṃ suptotthitaṃ vāpi hanti sā pūrvaśabditā ||
children.translated_text: and kills an animal asleep or just risen from sleep, that is the one named before.

children.text: te ca dve saikataprāye sānūpe vātha yatnataḥ
children.translated_text: Those two are especially successful with care in sandy terrain or in marshy ground
during the rainy season; at other times they again involve excessive fatigue.
Where, on barren ground and similar places, dogs brought near with a target in view

children.text: gṛhṇanti śaśakādīṃś ca śvānaḥ śvagaṇikā smṛtā ||
children.translated_text: catch hares and the like, that is remembered as <s>śvagaṇikā</s>.
The dogs' easy surrounding, and success or failure when the hare leaps,
through falling and springing up, are two forms that produce laughter and satisfaction.
When those dogs rush back, roaring loudly with a growl,
then, at the proper time, with enough ferocity for that, tooth against tooth and claw against claw,
two by two or three by three, by handlers skilled in releasing the leash from an open space,
the release of the dogs toward the target brings about its success.

children.text: tasyāṃ śarāṇāṃ sahasā mokṣo nānyatra śasyate
children.translated_text: In that method, sudden release of arrows is not commended elsewhere,
except after removing a boar that is attacking, for the success of the hounds.
But even a club, if useful, should be employed against hares and the like.
Thus this too is proclaimed to be a source of pleasures.

children.text: asyā eva bhidā kāpi kṛṣṇasāre rurau hi yaḥ
children.translated_text: Some subdivision of this same method applies to the black antelope and indeed to the ruru deer:

children.text: moko'tirasakṛd yena rajjvā moko'pi sa smṛtaḥ ||
children.translated_text: the repeated release by which there is intense sport, and even the release by rope, is remembered as that.

children.text: yasyāṃ tantrairdvidhā muktāḥ patatriṣu patanti ca
children.translated_text: Where hawks, released in two ways by means of devices,
fall upon birds, that very delightful method is called <s>śyenapāta</s>, the falcon-strike.

children.text: śyenapātā mṛgavyeti svairaṃ vānyasya vā bhavet
children.translated_text: Whether <s>śyenapāta</s> is hunting, either in itself or in relation to another, may be considered freely.
If it is hunting in itself for forest creatures, the term hunting would be meaningless.
If it is meaningful because hawks that eat hares seize deer and the like,
then why is that term not again applied to lions and other such animals?
Where other living beings are repeatedly sought for many purposes,

children.text: sā mṛgavyeti nirdiṣṭā sā tiraścāṃ na vidyate ||
children.translated_text: that is designated hunting; it is not found among animals.
They harm only for meat sufficient to fill their own bellies,
and no other purpose is connected with them.
The purpose of hunting is not merely for meat alone,
because there is also the obtaining of pearl, hide, and the like, and of musk and similar products.
Elephant-captures too are seen; therefore, for the accomplishment of many purposes,
the class of living beings is sought out, and so it is called hunting.

children.text: ato nṛbhiḥ prayuktānāṃ teṣāṃ pāto'tra kathyate
children.translated_text: Therefore their strike, when employed by men, is described here,
and thus this eighth kind of hunting has been explained as <s>śyenapāta</s>.

children.text: etasyā viśadatayā kilāṣṭa bhedā nirdiṣṭāḥ punarapare hyavāntarā ye
children.translated_text: Thus, for the sake of clarity, its eight divisions have been stated; and whatever further minor varieties there are,

children.text: te sarve rasajananāya naikarūpāḥ kalpyante vihitavidhānasamprayogāt ||
children.translated_text: all of them, being of many forms, are devised for the generation of relish through the application of the prescribed procedure.

children.text: iti śrīrudradevaviracite śyainike śāstre mṛgayāvivecanastṛtīyaḥ paricchedaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Thus ends the third section, the examination of hunting, in the <s>Śyainikaśāstra</s> composed by the illustrious <s>Rudradeva</s>.
That practice, endowed with the procedures beginning with release and marked by the characteristics of falconry,
and established through means beginning with gaining trust, is now explained.
Release is said to be of two kinds, divided into hand-release and fist-release.
Where the noose on the falcon's foot is pressed with all the fingers,

children.text: vidhāya kriyate moko hastamokaḥ sa ucyate
children.translated_text: and release is then made, that is called hand-release.
This same release is taught for kuhyas and the like, and is also praised for residences and similar places.
Having placed the bird, wrapped in cloth, upon the palm according to one's strength,
a casting off as if unattached is called fist-release.
A release is praised in two forms: unattached, light, with exhilaration, and proceeding easily after what has gone before,

children.text: praśasyate dvidhā moko dūre dūre yathāyatham ||
children.translated_text: farther and farther, according to each proper occasion.
Their gaining of trust is first described here according to rule.
At the beginning, the skilled man should open the eyes by unsewing them.

children.text: yathā na mukhamīkṣeta yathā vā pratiśīrṣakaiḥ
children.translated_text: He should ensure that the bird does not look at his face, or else he should use coverings for the head,
and he should not make it hear a sound until five days have passed.
Then, night after night, with a little light from lamps and the like,
he should uncover the eyes and wash them in pleasantly cool water.

children.text: kiṃcit kiṃcit paricayaṃ kārayet śrāvayet vacaḥ
children.translated_text: Little by little he should make it familiar, and should make it hear his voice.
Thus, in due order, by touching with the hand and so on, and by coaxing speech,
by giving water and meat at the appointed time, and by soothing attentions,
by relieving shade and heat, and gradually by freeing the eyes,
one should determine whether they are attached or unattached from their behavior.

children.text: netre nimīlya tiṣṭhanti caikapādena vai yadā ||
children.translated_text: When they stand with their eyes closed, indeed on one foot,
and scratch with the beak and shake the wings and shoulders,
and when they look at the face and direct a gentle gaze,

children.text: tadā raktāstu vijñeyā viraktāstvanyathā tu te
children.translated_text: then they should be known as attached; but otherwise they are disaffected.
Having recognized the attached ones, while they are fitted with a cord, one should call them with meat and the like.
Gradually one should increase the ground distance, and call them twice and three times.

children.text: yadāhvāne no vilambaṃ kuryus tiryaṅ na vā gatim ||
children.translated_text: When, on being called, they make no delay and do not go sideways,

children.text: na māṃsādestathā kṛṣṭiṃ tadā rajjvā vināhvayet
children.translated_text: nor pull at the meat and the like, then one should call them without the cord.
Then, having set them upon a tree or the like, one should cause them to be called gradually.
Again, one should make them seize birds such as <s>kalaviṅka</s> and pigeon,
as appropriate, in order to remind them of their earlier training.
Those that do not become obedient by this gradual method
one should bring under control by excessive wakefulness, very frequent contact with the hand, and pulling.

children.text: teṣāṃ jātyanurūpā ca rañjanāya kriyā matā
children.translated_text: The procedure for pleasing them is considered to accord with their species.
Therefore I shall next explain separately the distinction of the species of <s>śyena</s>s.

children.text: kṛṣṇākṣā pāṭalākṣā ca jātī dve prasphuṭāntare
children.translated_text: The black-eyed and the reddish-eyed are two species, clearly distinct from one another.
And among them many other subordinate divisions are also observed.
The names of those born in the two principal species are stated.
<s>kuhī</s>s, <s>śaśāda</s>s, <s>caraka</s>s, <s>vaharī</s>s, and <s>lagara</s>s, likewise,
and another, the <s>pakṣakalikā</s>, and another, the <s>turumutī</s>;
with the same number of male forms, this is the group born from the black-eyed species.
This group is to be trained by excessive wakefulness, while being fed with water and meat.
A stone should be cast at the mouth, and likewise when there is biting of the hand and so on.
Its visual confidence arises very quickly,

children.text: ābhyantarastu kṛcchreṇa tasmād yuktyā vaśaṃ nayet ||
children.translated_text: but inner trust only with difficulty; therefore one should bring it under control by skillful means.
One should arrange calling by tying the wings, or with a cloth.
When it has come, food should be given, so that its hope is not frustrated.

children.text: vāgdaṇḍaiś cārthadaṇḍaiś ca kiṃcid āśvāsanais tathā
children.translated_text: By verbal punishments, by material punishments, and also by a little encouragement,
the wicked are kept under one's control; just so is this group.
When overfed it becomes deformed; when over-emaciated, powerless.
This group is remembered as being just like a low servant.
By means that increase expectation, and by gifts suited to their work,

children.text: rañjitā rañjanāyālaṃ bhṛtyā iva bhavanti te ||
children.translated_text: when pleased, they become sufficient for pleasing, like servants.
In being called from afar, in a long swoop, and in seizing a large target,

children.text: praśasta eṣa hi gaṇo dvitīyaḥ kathyate'dhunā ||
children.translated_text: this group is excellent. Now the second is described.
<s>patra</s>, <s>vāja</s>, and <s>chada</s> are expressions stated as synonyms.
By this, the general possession of wings belongs to birds.

children.text: yathāśvatthāmni karṇe ca bhīṣme pārthe ca rukmiṇi
children.translated_text: Just as, in the case of <s>Aśvatthāman</s>, <s>Karṇa</s>, <s>Bhīṣma</s>, <s>Pārtha</s>, and <s>Rukmiṇī</s>,
though left-handed skill is common, because of excellence the name applies to <s>Arjuna</s>,
so too, although wingedness is common to all birds,
the words <s>patrin</s> and <s>vājin</s> indicate distinction in the <s>śyena</s>.
<s>vāja</s>s, <s>vāsa</s>s, <s>vesara</s>s, and <s>sicāna</s>s are fourfold.
<s>jūra</s>s, <s>ceṭa</s>s, and <s>dhūtiṭuna</s>s are their male forms.
Among both groups, the superiority of the females is strong,
in bodily build, courage, price, and excellence of wings and flight and the like.
Yet because <s>vāja</s> and the others are principal, they are designated in the masculine gender.
The <s>vājin</s>s are fivefold; their separate characteristics are stated.
One is thin in form, with eyes like a crane, and with white and black locks,
on the body and also on the thighs; it is proclaimed easy to train.

children.text: yaś cakravākasaṃsthānaś cakrāṅgaḥ sa ca kīrtitaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The one whose build is like a <s>cakravāka</s> is called <s>cakrāṅga</s>.
The long one, black in build and resembling a heron, is remembered as <s>kālaka</s>.
It comes to trust only after a long time, and even when deeply attached it becomes disaffected.

children.text: yaḥ sarvāṅge himaprakhyo haṃsavājaḥ sa kathyate
children.translated_text: The one whose whole body is snow-like is called the <s>haṃsavāja</s>.

children.text: sa yatra pūjitastiṣṭhet kalyāṇaṃ tatra jāyate ||
children.translated_text: Wherever it remains honored, good fortune arises there.
One should protect it carefully and should not employ it in dice-games and the like.
By its touch fevers, including quartan fevers and others, perish.
The one on whose tail-feathers and other feathers there appears a line like an aśvattha leaf,
that king of <s>vāja</s>s is called <s>mahārāvaṇa</s>.
It is obtained through a great accumulation of merit and is an object of wonder.
Because of its cry among flocks of birds, it is called <s>mahārāvaṇa</s>.
<s>auraṅganā</s>s, <s>dhāvana</s>s, <s>pratiṣṭhāna</s>s, and likewise
<s>śikāra</s>s: thus the species of the <s>vāsa</s>s is said to be fourfold.
The <s>auraṅganā</s>s are of many kinds, both high and low,
differing in valor, courage, and also in colors.
The <s>dhāvana</s>s have small bodies, are delicate, and are especially swift.

children.text: patraprāyāḥ pratiṣṭhānā mandā vege ca sāhase ||
children.translated_text: The <s>pratiṣṭhāna</s>s are mostly wing; they are slow in speed and courage.
They are healthy, compact in body, and born in the land of the <s>vāja</s>s.
By color they are remembered as whitish, ochre-like, and blackish.
The <s>śikāra</s>s are well-tempered, swift, fierce, and violently courageous,
as if dripping nectar by the excellence of the form of their eyes.
They are obtained through extraordinary merit and are endowed with training and refinement.
One should not distress them with the hardships of excessive wakefulness, but should fondle them repeatedly.
Only when well nourished should one employ them in hunting for the mind's delight.
The vesaras are of three kinds; their separate names are stated.
The coarse, inferior one is the māṇika, while the cūlikāṅka is middling.
The pure one is like the vāsā, even when there is superiority in wing and boldness.
Because they are born in many regions, and because of the nature of those regions,
the sicās are remembered as being of many sorts, with various forms and behaviors.
The male characteristics of these too are recognized by their marks.
But, from fear of prolixity, they are not displayed here.
A head shaped like the hood of a serpent is praised, and so too an elevated neck,
long wings, and a broad chest, for all birds.
Likewise the two leg-tubes should be short, round, full, and well joined.
The two feet are considered good when the toes are long and the joints are closely connected.
Their claws should be raised upward, and their sitting posture should have the form of a svastika.
These are understood to be their general marks.
The vāsā has a sweet voice and is fortunate; the vājī is mute and very beautiful.

children.text: kuhī yasyāḥ kaṇḍikā hi karṇāntā rajatākṛtiḥ ||
children.translated_text: The kuhī is that whose kaṇḍikā reaches to the ears and has a silvery appearance.
Hawks, nourished by honorable treatment of their wings and won over by fond care,
come to the attainment of desired aims, like good ministers.
No one except the bird and its trainer knows the peerless excellence of intelligence and skill,
just as no one other than one versed in the arrangement of royal policy knows it.
Where there is the calming of what has been obtained and reflection on what has not been obtained,

children.text: duṣṭānāṃ karṣaṇaṃ yuktyā vinītānāṃ ca poṣaṇam ||
children.translated_text: the weakening of the wicked by strategy and the nourishing of the disciplined,
the increasing of energy in those who have done their work by fulfilling their desires,
constant pleasing and protection, and testing of the attached and the unattached,
the winning of trust, distrust, and observation of movements of the eyes,
knowledge of what is to be accomplished and the means, and discernment of what is possible and impossible,
and, after knowing this, appointing the fit and turning away the unfit,

children.text: ityādyūhyā guṇā ye ca rājadharmme pradarśitāḥ ||
children.translated_text: and whatever other qualities are to be inferred that are taught in royal <s>dharma</s>,

children.text: tatra te śyainike śāstre vicīyante manīṣibhiḥ
children.translated_text: there, in the <s>śyainika</s> treatise, those qualities are investigated by the wise.

children.text: yathāvakāśaṃ hi rasā nāṭyādau ye vinirmitāḥ ||
children.translated_text: For, according to occasion, the sentiments that are fashioned in drama and the like are there.

Those for whom hunting is desired should study this <s>Śyainika</s>, profound through the cultivation of many such sentiments, easy to understand because it can be pleasantly used by everyone from commoners onward,

children.text: saṃkṣiptayuktiracitaṃ pariśīlayantu te śyainikaṃ tu mṛgayābhimatā hi yeṣām ||
children.translated_text: and composed with concise reasoning.

children.text: iti śrīrudradevaviracite śyainike śāstre śyenānāṃ vivecanaṃ paricchedaḥ caturthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Thus ends the fourth section, the discrimination of hawks, in the <s>Śyainikaśāstra</s> composed by the illustrious <s>Rudradeva</s>.
Now the measure of their food-quantity is stated,
as well as their seasonal regimen and the examination and restraint of diseases.
The measure of pure meat consisting of twenty-five ṭaṅkas
should apply to the kuhī, caraka, vāja, and vaharī birds.
The hare-eaters are not fit for a small measure, and likewise are unable to bear fasting.

children.text: jātimātreṇa nirdeśāsteṣāṃ krīḍā tu no hitā ||
children.translated_text: The prescriptions concerning them are by species alone; sport with them is not beneficial.

children.text: te pañcahīnāṃ tāsāṃ tu puṃvyaktīnāṃ prayojayet
children.translated_text: For their male specimens one should use a measure five less than that.
For the pakṣakākalikā the measure should then be five less than that.
Thereafter one should prescribe two less for the vāsās, and again two less than that.
For pure vesaras and cūlāṅkas the measures have been stated before.
That much quantity should be arranged for the sicās according to what suits them.
For the turumutīs, however, it is fixed at nine ṭaṅkas.
For ceṭāṭonas and dhūtikās one should arrange a lean measure in the order of one, two, and three.
This measure should be arranged and applied to them twice.
The arrangement should be made as is appropriate, like the wage and food of a servant.
Even delay in time is commended, though it can produce disturbance in the system.
Likewise, for these birds too, delay in the timing of meals is not praised.
Irregularity in the measure also would bring about defect.
This measure has been declared for those assigned to hunting exercise.
For releasing the wings from Jyaistha onward, one should arrange another measure.
In summer, the quarters are scorched by the heat of the fierce sun.
The trees too do not shine, being without shelter with their leaves withered.
Storm-winds, turbid with masses of dust, blow everywhere.
The waters of the rivers flow as if boiling.
Because of the sap and dust, hot and hard to touch, living beings here
are seen to be without hostility, without energy, and as if fevered.
Birds cry out in high, repeated, pitiful sounds.
Especially those familiar with the slopes of the snowy mountain, adorned with spotless rocks washed by flowing water,
covered with fine grass resembling split sapphires,
and with breezes made fragrant by flowing resin from sarala trees,
for those birds accustomed to such places,
summer, like a forest fire, becomes hard to bear.
Therefore one should apply treatments that relieve heat.
For them, on the top of a palace whose interior is whitened with lime,
cooled by showers of water released from mechanical devices at the edges,
and with air produced from afar by people holding fans,
binding should be done in a secluded place, screened with netting against flies.
Or else it should be done on a well-built garden terrace, protected by good guards,
cooled by the water of flowing channels and by densely rising trees,
continually free from the passage of the fierce sun's rays.
Or binding is desired in an underground chamber made fragrant by water placed over uśīra grass,
beautiful all around with barley sprouts arising from irrigated basins,
pleasant, and free from biting flies and mosquitoes.
One should arrange a place that delights the eyes and satisfies the nose,
with a good circulation of air and with open space.

children.text: naikatra bahavaḥ sthāpyāḥ dvitrāḥ sthāpyāḥ pṛthak pṛthak ||
children.translated_text: Many should not be placed in one place; two or three should be placed separately.

children.text: na ca tebhyaḥ suśītāmbu vāravāraṃ pradarśayet
children.translated_text: And one should not repeatedly show them very cold water.
The meat of horses and the like, of sparrows and the like, should not be very stale.
Light, palatable meat should be given in such a way that it is digested.
For their nourishment, one should then increase the measure little by little.
For bathing, small vessels filled with water should be placed in front of them.
If they vomit up the meat they have eaten, then this is the remedy for them:
fenugreek powder is recommended with fresh butter from a she-buffalo.
If what they have eaten is digested, then meat should be given to them.
It should be freshly taken, sprinkled with wine-water, and joined with <s>candrāṅka</s>.
Or else fire-powder should be given for calming that condition.
Or it may be mixed with hemp-juice; afterwards one should make them drink hot water.

children.text: yuktyā yathā nodvijeran yuktiḥ sarvatra sādhikā
children.translated_text: This should be done with skill, so that they are not distressed; skill is everywhere the chief means.
If they become emaciated, then meat mixed with women's breast-milk
or with fresh butter from a cow is considered to be given.
For awakening hunger, it may again be given with clove or with human urine.
In this way, having gradually produced an increase of hunger, one should nourish them fully
by daily increases of measure and by very cooling treatments.
Now when the clouds make their sound and the sky is lit by flashes of lightning,
when there is delight for all embodied beings from the fragrance produced by jasmine,
when it is noisy with the croaking of frogs and peacocks perform their dance,
when the wind, announcing the fragrance of kadamba, blows everywhere,
when the water of rivers is muddy because torrents are moving everywhere,
and when the rainy season has arrived, vocal with the chirping of crickets,
then one should tend them in just such a way
that, having become well nourished, they quickly abandon their old wings and take on new ones, like snakes their skin.
If they overrun the proper time for releasing the feathers, meat should be given.
Some also know lizard meat as useful for releasing the feathers.
Barbarian peoples give an extract of cow, buffalo, and the like.
Because of cruelty and because it produces excessive speed and other effects, this is not praised.
If worms cause the feathers to fall, then this is the remedy:
one should administer equal parts of vidanga, fire-powder, and musk.
Or else, for large birds, the amount is two rattis of rock salt;
for small ones, half a ratti, together with meat, for three days.
Hawks well trained by those who know them become givers of delight.
Therefore, because men have previously seen faults that obstruct pleasure,
diseases arise even among them here; and so, for their pacification,
I shall briefly describe for their restraint the sequence of medicines.
The irregular functioning of breath is said to be fourfold, called <s>śākhā</s>.
One kind arises from injury, another from phlegm, and another from bile.

children.text: kṣaiṇyajānyā śoṣiteti kṛcchrasādhyā tu sā smṛtā
children.translated_text: Another, born of wasting, is called the dried-up type, and it is remembered as difficult to cure.
For these birds afflicted by <s>śākhā</s>-pain, a place in darkness and extreme solitude

children.text: iṣyate sthānam alpālpam āmiṣaṃ sāmbu dāpayet
children.translated_text: is recommended; one should give them meat with water, little by little.
In the injury-born type, owl-pair meat should be given; and on the body too, if there is pain,
one should apply turmeric with skill, and sprinkle with stale water.

children.text: śleṣmaje māricaṃ cūrṇaṃ nasye prāk saṃprayojayet ||
children.translated_text: In the phlegmatic type, one should first use powdered black pepper as a nasal treatment.
Meat should be given together with powder of the bark of <s>śigru</s>, and one should make them drink hot water.
Musk too should be given for pacifying the complications of that condition.
In the bilious type, a pill made with equal portions of camphor, clove, vetiver, and sandalwood
should be given, according to proper method, just before the meat.

children.text: paścānmāsaṃ varttikāder deyam alpaṃ savāri ca
children.translated_text: Afterwards, for a month, a little meat of quail and the like should be given, along with water.
The type born of wasting is said to be hard to overcome; still, the treatment is stated.
Indeed, even well-arranged actions bear fruit when a remainder of life remains.
Meat of sparrows and the like sprinkled with human blood is recommended.
Or else one should use what is available at that time for feeding and care.

children.text: kiṭer api prayoktavyam alpam alpaṃ yathābalam ||
children.translated_text: Even meat of insects should be used, little by little, according to their strength.
One should give the birds meat mixed with fresh butter from a cow,
and, with due method, make them drink hot water afterwards.
One should administer water mixed with camphor from time to time.

children.text: athaiṣāṃ śākhināṃ śastā mimāyī yā prakīrtyate ||
children.translated_text: Now for these <s>śākhin</s> birds, the medicine called <s>mimāyī</s> is proclaimed as beneficial.
For large, dark-eyed ones, the dose should be three rattis.
For the small ones among them, one should prescribe half that dose.

children.text: sthūlānāṃ pāṭalākṣāṇāṃ mātrā dve kṛṣṇale smṛtā
children.translated_text: For large, reddish-eyed ones, the dose is remembered as two kṛṣṇalas.

children.text: sūkṣmāṇāṃ kṛṣṇalaikā tu mātrā bhavati cauṣadhe ||
children.translated_text: For small ones, one kṛṣṇala is the medicinal dose.
Breast-milk mixed with hemp-juice should be combined with meat.
And one should anoint their eyes daily with cumin chewed by the teeth.
Exactly twenty-one days are prescribed for all <s>śākhin</s> birds.
<s>Māgadhī</s>, turmeric, <s>vola</s>, <s>mimāyī</s>, alkali, and <s>pāṭalā</s>:
the powder of these, strained through cloth and mixed with goat's milk,
should be given to the <s>śākhin</s> birds with meat for twenty-one days.
Powder of the root-bark of <s>śigru</s>, mixed with the latex of <s>arka</s>,
should be given with meat to all <s>śākhin</s> birds for seven days.

children.text: patanti tāpāt dhūmācca ghātāt puṣpāṇi netrayoḥ
children.translated_text: From heat, from smoke, and from injury, white films fall upon the eyes.
One should fill the eyes with fine powder of the root of wood-sorrel.
Thus the hawk is freed from the white films in eighteen days.
Or else turmeric, neem leaves, and black peppers,
mixed in equal measure with myrobalan, long pepper, nut-grass, and vidanga,
should be made into a pill with goat's urine and dried in the shade.
For reddish eye-disease it should be applied with honey; for white films, with breast-milk.
The plaster, as prepared by <s>Rudra</s>, certainly destroys it.
From irregularity in drinking and eating, and from an increase of bile in the eyes,

children.text: śophaḥ saṃjāyate vaktre tathā pākaśca durdharaḥ ||
children.translated_text: swelling arises on the face, and also a suppuration that is hard to bear.
Likewise, from an excess of phlegm it becomes difficult to cure.
Powder of challikā from a milky tree, mixed with sesame oil,
should be given with meat in the former type; a plaster is also recommended.
But in the phlegmatic type the head should be pierced with a heated iron probe.
For suppuration of the mouth, meat mixed with human urine is recommended.
After that, washing should also be done for cleansing the mouth.
Because of the hardness caused by binding, and through fear, by frequent jumping up,

children.text: jāyate savraṇaḥ śophaḥ padayor gardabhīti sā ||
children.translated_text: an ulcerated swelling arises on the feet; that is called gardabhī.
When the same condition of the feet has passed too long, it is called cāndī.
One should mix pippala and udumbara in milk and smear
the feet every day for seven days, in order to calm gardabhī.

children.text: śāntimabhyeti teṣāṃ hi viṭpralepena vā punaḥ ||
children.translated_text: For in these birds it becomes pacified; or again by a plaster of dung.
But after applying a leech, together with turmeric and rock salt,

children.text: navanītena tu svinnāṃ liptvā vastreṇa veṣṭayet ||
children.translated_text: and steaming it with fresh butter, one should smear it and wrap it with cloth.
For three days; having removed that, one should again apply the plaster in this way.
By the plaster, in twelve days even cāndī is plainly removed.
When a bird is observed to be diminished in strength and color because of a blow,
this medicine, which will now be stated, should be given to it without negligence.

children.text: dve niśe tutthakaṃ bhārgī madanaṃ cārkajaṃ payaḥ
children.translated_text: Two niśās, tuttha, bhārgī, madana, and milk from the arka plant
should all together be mixed with ghee and with meat.
It should be given according to proper measure for a period of twenty-one days.
From eating wet, stale, and hard-to-digest meat,

children.text: nānāvidhā hi kṛmayo dṛśyante teṣu yojayet
children.translated_text: various worms are indeed seen in them; for those one should apply this:
two parts viḍaṅga and one part musk
should be mixed and given to drink with due method, for the calming of that disease.

children.text: bhayādasnāyināṃ gātre likṣā yūkāḥ patanti ca ||
children.translated_text: Through fear and because they have not bathed, nits and lice fall upon their bodies.
For their destruction, dusting with powder of māgadhī is beneficial.
Also, having ground the root-bark of bilva with water mixed with cow urine,

children.text: tallepādeva naśyanti yūkā likhyā na saṃśayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: by that plaster alone lice and nits perish; there is no doubt.

children.text: ityagadair uditair upacāraiḥ saṃvihitaiḥ suhitaiśca yathāvat
children.translated_text: Thus, by the remedies and treatments that have been stated, properly arranged and beneficial,
when he sees them well nourished because they are free from disease, he should then train them for hunting.

children.text: iti śrīrudradevaviracite śyainike śāstre cikitsādhikāraparicchedaḥ pañcamaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Thus ends the fifth section, the chapter on treatment, in the <s>Śyainikaśāstra</s> composed by the illustrious <s>Rudradeva</s>.
Now, by such medicines and by the strengthening measures previously mentioned,
when he observes them to be delighted, well nourished, and adorned with new plumage,
shining with wings resembling blue sapphire,
marked with rows of broad thigh-feathers like nets of pearls,
resembling snakes that have sloughed their skins, fitted with silk leashes,
made variegated by clusters of jeweled neck-bands and foot-straps,
and noisy with the sound of small bells, then on an auspicious day
he should again make them attached according to the previously stated method and call them back.
For reminding them of their earlier training, when the birds are controlled by cords,
one skilled in protecting the wings should teach them circling flight.
Those hawks that were formerly obtained from nests and raised in bondage,
being unpracticed in training,
a wise man should train in many ways in the flying of birds, by gradual increases in skill.

children.text: suśiṣyā iva te śyenāḥ śikṣāṃ gṛhṇanti satvaram ||
children.translated_text: Like good pupils, those hawks quickly grasp the training.
For hawks that are properly and well trained, like winds,
there is nothing impossible, nothing unattainable among suitable objects.
Young men with polished earrings should hold them on their hands,
well dressed, wearing fine garments, and trained in many ways every day.
Having observed the clarity of their training, then the lord himself
should go out to see the sport on a day appointed for the hunt.
Starting from the first watch of the night, and early in the morning, with the rising light,
he should go when the sun is covered by autumn clouds.
Having sent many troops far afield and blocked other passages,
he himself should be surrounded mostly by a few renowned and trusted heroes.
With all their skill in movement set upon the falconer's cords,
and with their placing of steps marked by the sound of good reins,
he should be carried by his own horses, joined by the hawk-bearers,
untiring, at the proper time, in the shade of great mountains.
Or else he may go hunting in the last part of the day.

children.text: śaratkāle pṛṣṭhato'rkaṃ kṛtvā dūre tu no hitam ||
children.translated_text: In the autumn season he should keep the sun behind him; going far is not beneficial.
If he approaches hunting in a valley, then on all sides
he should send foot-soldiers through mountain hollows and the intervening places.
Stationed there, they should watch everywhere for the birds:
where they fly up, where they fall elsewhere, and the hidden places in between.

children.text: samāyāṃ bhuvi vistāro mārgaṇe sādināṃ bhavet
children.translated_text: On level ground, the spread in searching should belong to the horsemen;

children.text: viṣamāyāṃ tu pattīnāṃ girikūṭe śunāṃ punaḥ ||
children.translated_text: on uneven ground to the footmen, and on mountain peaks to the dogs.

children.text: madhye śyenadharo netā pārśvayordvau ca sainikau
children.translated_text: In the middle should be the leader bearing the hawk, and on the two sides two soldiers.
A circle is said to consist of twenty-one horsemen.
The left-hand man, with his eye directed by the leader, at a distance of one vyāma,
should move in the circle, while the people on both sides are evenly divided.

children.text: ā pūrvād aiśvarīm āśām adhimoktum athārhati
children.translated_text: Then he is able to release it toward the northeastern direction from the east,
so that the falconer does not cause alarm to the quarry of the two.
And he who has many hawks, and likewise horsemen and the like,

children.text: saṃcārayet sa parito maṇḍalāni pṛthak pṛthak ||
children.translated_text: should set them moving all around, in separate circles, each apart.
The hawker, stationed in the middle of the lord's circle, without an order
must not release the bird, even when the target is very near, while keeping his position unshaken.
In a circle there should be one <s>baharī</s>, one <s>kuhyā</s>, and three horsemen;

children.text: vāsādyāḥ pañcaṣāḥ śastāḥ kramo moke puroditaḥ ||
children.translated_text: five or six <s>vāsā</s> and the others are recommended; the order of release has been stated before.
He should keep his own men half a krośa away, one circle separate from another,
so that there will be no danger from the mingling of the <s>kuhyā</s> and the others with the <s>vāsā</s> and the others.

children.text: vanyānāṃ tu śaśādīnāṃ trāsanāya puraiva hi
children.translated_text: For frightening wild animals such as hares and the like, beforehand indeed
drawn swords should be made ready, or spears should be held on all sides.
Many fletched missiles should be held by disciplined attendants who know the right time,
all around a powerful hawker.
While searching, slow movement of the circle is always desired;
in tracking after a strike, still slower movement is desired.
Those who go before the riders, the men with canes, are also drivers;
by releasing from the fist they should cast <s>ṭona</s> birds and the like at quails and similar quarry.
Because of their speed, their courses are hard to perceive; they too, against birds that fall obliquely,
give fullness to the rasa by taking note of the cries <s>cīcī</s> and <s>kucī</s> and so forth.
If the lord, his heart drawn by that rasa,
should make those very birds play, then the knowledgeable cane-bearers should be treated with respect.
Making cane-blows all around, against those that move slowly,
they should make partridges and the like rise up, and should drive their movements in that direction.
Where a bird has fallen once and does not spring up again,
there, after searching with a leashed dog, one should let it go.
The lord must be attentive, for that bird is about to fly up;
with such sweet speeches and the like they should instruct the lord accordingly.
The release of a <s>kuhyā</s> against a crane or a curlew brings the raudra rasa (furious mood),
where there is a chase like that of two winged mountains.
Having swooped down, with a cruel shriek caused by the thrusting of its claws,
and then turning back to strike with its fierce beak, it is a furious battle.
But against very distant birds such as herons and <s>dātyūha</s> birds,

children.text: lakṣye moko baharyā hi janayatyadbhutaṃ rasam ||
children.translated_text: the release of the <s>baharī</s> at the target produces the adbhuta rasa (wonder).
Where birds, terrified by the sound of the wind from its speed, fall from the sky,
like trees with wings and mountain-peaks cut off, what wonder is there in that?
Taking up a lovely young creature, devouring its still-breathing limbs,
the irresistible <s>carakha</s> produces the bībhatsa rasa (disgust) in full.
From the wing-speed of <s>ṭona</s> birds and the like, some <s>kecuka</s> birds and others hide away;
hemmed in among the thickets, they display the bhayānaka rasa (terror).
A <s>bharadvāja</s> bird, deeply hidden, then chattering much in high and low tones,
coming into sight of the target freely, becomes an occasion for the hāsya rasa (comic mood).
Then, when they are frightened and hidden, but are targets by their voices,
one who desires amusement should make use of pellet-weapons.
Falling upon targets from far away and seizing them in the proper place,
skilled in making them lifeless, the <s>vājī</s> becomes an occasion for the vīra rasa (heroic mood).
Upward attack, level attack, and downward attack: thus there are three
fields of rasa for the <s>vāja</s> birds in seizing excellent quarry.
When the quarry hides below like a shadow, and likewise when the target goes upward suddenly,
the leap and arrow-like fall of the upward attack is rich in rasa.
Because it pursues evenly, whether the target is visible or invisible,

children.text: daṇḍavat patanaṃ lakṣye samākrāntiḥ samā matā ||
children.translated_text: a staff-like fall upon the target is regarded as an even level attack.
When the quarry is moving low, from fear, and from above like a thunderbolt
the bird falls on the target in fury, that downward attack is very difficult.
Thus, by following targets, by circling many times,
and by excessive confidence, the <s>vāja</s> birds have reached excellence among winged creatures.
By leaping up again and again and falling, by seizing and casting down,

children.text: mallā iva vidagdhānāṃ haranti prasabhaṃ manaḥ ||
children.translated_text: like wrestlers, they forcibly carry away the minds of connoisseurs.
When birds moving in pairs are involved, at the capture of one, the cry of the other
wherever it sounds there makes the karuṇa rasa (pathos) grow tender.
There a full śṛṅgāra rasa (erotic mood) is seen in the hero in two ways:
when the target is reached, it has the form of enjoyment; when it is not reached, it is otherwise.
By horripilation as occasion allows, joy, tears, stillness, faltering voice,
anxiety, lament, change of color, and other states, it manifests inner feeling.
The rasa in hunting is superior even to that from union with women;
by it a doe-eyed woman, herself frightened, fully brings her husband under her power.
Leaving his beloved clinging to his neck, even on winter nights,

children.text: nābhisāraṃ narāḥ kuryuryadi neṣṭā ca sā bhavet ||
children.translated_text: men would not go to an assignation if that hunting were not dear to them.
Now the release of the <s>vāsā</s> and the others too, with modes such as taking shelter and leaving shelter,
follows śṛṅgāra, because it makes an impetuous embrace.
When the winged creatures are seized, their body-hairs fall from the sky,
and create the illusion of masses of flowers released by delighted Indra.

children.text: ye vimuktā nije lakṣye dūre dūre skhalanti na
children.translated_text: Those hunters whose birds, released at their own targets far away, do not miss
are vessels worthy of praise, not the others.
The speed and repeated aiming of hunters, twice and three times,
in the taking of partridges and the like: by whom could that be adequately described?
So too among web-footed birds, in pools and lakes,
followed by advance scouts, one should release <s>kuhyā</s> birds and the like.

children.text: tatra sambhūya mokṣo'pi viśrambhaṃ ye gatā mithaḥ
children.translated_text: There, even a combined release of those that have reached mutual confidence

children.text: teṣāṃ praśasyate dikṣu kavīnāṃ viplavāya tu ||
children.translated_text: is praised in the quarters, but only to the confusion of poets.
The beating of drums should be done so that the birds give up the water,
so that the hawks may easily seize those that have been dislodged from their own places.

children.text: ye nāṭyabandhakuśalairvitataprapañcaiḥ saṃdarśitāḥ kila rasāḥ samayaṃ vibhajya
children.translated_text: The rasas which, it is said, are displayed by experts in dramatic composition through elaborately extended arrangements, dividing them according to occasion,

children.text: ekatra te samakameva rasā anūnā dṛśyanta eva kṛtibhirmṛgayāvihāre ||
children.translated_text: all those rasas, complete and all together in one place, are actually seen by skilled men in the sport of hunting.

children.text: iti śrīrudradevaviracite śyainike śāstre śyenapāteti kartavyatā paricchedaḥ ṣaṣṭhaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Thus ends the sixth section, called "The Procedure for the Hawk's Descent," in the <s>Śyainikaśāstra</s> composed by the illustrious <s>Rudradeva</s>.
Having thus sported all around, when he is tired he deserves rest,
in deep shade, fanned by breezes rich with the fragrance of lotuses.
Then, after returning, all the others who move about in the hunting circles,
their chief men, and whatever has been acquired by the leader,
bringing that from the hunt, and also the behavior of the hawks and the rest,
should report everything before the lord for his amusement.
Through that report, the lord too should give honors and the like
to the falconers and to the various men moving in those circles, for the increase of their enthusiasm.
Having fed and watered the hawks and horses, and tied them in pleasant shade,
he himself, in a secluded place, should undergo the act of having his limbs massaged.
Listening to the unsurpassed calls of gracefully moving swans,
and to lute music and other things charming to the heart, he should pass some time.
Then, bathed, anointed, bright with pearl garlands and garments,
having performed his daily rite and properly adorned with fine flowers,
his fatigue removed by a pure drink of <s>cīnī</s> with the belly of a swan,
wearing it, with his mind serene and approved by the physicians,
furnished with a ring bearing <s>Garuḍa</s>, attended by finger-skilled physicians,
after first giving to the horses and birds for the sake of examination,
he should eat foods brought by experts, and well-spitted meats,
and rice dishes white as jasmine, together with his attendants.
Then, having used betel and the like, when the sun's heat has become calm,
he should come back to his own residence, telling various kinds of stories.
"How was the crane, by the female messenger, through a side-story, and the very proud quail,
in many ways by this horse, struck down like grass and reeds?"
"By this hunt, we tell how the partridge was subdued;
by this falconer there was release, then a bursting forth full of delight."

children.text: tathādhamenāmunā tu tiryak kṣipto na cotthitaḥ
children.translated_text: "But by this inferior one it was thrown sideways and did not rise up;
this bird does not in that way meet with opposition."
One should avoid all meats, for <s>dharma</s> is prescribed here;
but meat is treated by all kings.
By those who had become the selves of all beings, both high and low,
by <s>Nābhāga</s>, by <s>Ambarīṣa</s>, and by great-souled <s>Rāma</s>,

children.text: ailena pṛthunā caiva vīrasenena caiva hi
children.translated_text: by <s>Aila</s> and <s>Pṛthu</s> too, and also by <s>Vīrasena</s>,

children.text: haryaśvena ca rājendra bhūpena bharatena ca ||
children.translated_text: and by <s>Haryaśva</s>, O king, and by King <s>Bharata</s>,

children.text: etaiścānyaiśca rājendra purā māṃsaṃ na bhakṣitam
children.translated_text: by these and by other kings, O king, meat was not eaten in former times;
in the autumnal bright fortnight they then attained heaven.

children.text: brahmaloke ca tiṣṭhanti kalpamānāḥ striyā vṛtāḥ
children.translated_text: And they dwell in <s>Brahmaloka</s>, honored and surrounded by women.
As hunting is prescribed there alone, elsewhere than at the autumn moonlight festival,
so, even when it is not forbidden at another time, one should avoid it there.
For by the great-souled <s>Agastya</s>, who desired the welfare of creatures,
wild animals, belonging to all the deities, dark in nature, were consecrated.
In autumn one should practice it with due method; in the cold season, according to one's wish;
but in spring especially, by those who desire strength and health.

children.text: dhanurvedābhyāsaḥ samavidhiranūnaśca laghutā gatergātrotsāhaḥ turagavihṛtau cātipaṭutā
children.translated_text: Practice in archery, a complete and even discipline, lightness of movement, bodily vigor, and great skill in moving on horseback,

children.text: tathā nīteryoge rasaparicayaścāpyanupamo mṛgavyāyāṃ kṣātro guṇasamudayo 'bhyasyata iva ||
children.translated_text: as well as training in policy and an incomparable acquaintance with the rasas: in hunting, the whole collection of kṣatriya qualities is, as it were, practiced.

children.text: iti śrīrudradevaviracite śyainike śāstre mṛgayānantaretikartavyatā paricchedaḥ saptamaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Thus ends the seventh section, called "The Procedure After Hunting," in the <s>Śyainikaśāstra</s> composed by the illustrious <s>Rudradeva</s>.
